chapter_title: Chương 21: Thử vận may, xe đạp biến xe máy.

segments.title: Chương 21: Thử vận may, xe đạp biến xe máy.
segments.content:
Tao Chenggang was engrossed, reading and thinking at the same time.

A full half hour passed before he put down the few A4 pages.

Chen Guiliang immediately took them back, folded them twice, and stuffed them into his pocket.

Seeing this, Tao Chenggang couldn't help but laugh, then he asked, "These ideas of yours are very interesting. Why not approach a big company?"

Chen Guiliang said, "Those big companies, I don't even know which way their doors open. Even if I found some executive, they'd probably just steal my idea."

Tao Chenggang asked, "Aren't you afraid I'll steal yours?"

"Uncle said Boss Tao is a man of honor and definitely wouldn't do something so low," Chen Guiliang flattered with a smile, then added with a subtle threat, "If Boss Tao doesn't buy it, I'll just go try the big companies again."

Of course, Tao Chenggang could hear the underlying meaning. This was Chen Guiliang threatening him.

If he really decided to develop a game, he would have to worry about Chen Guiliang causing trouble. It would be a real headache if he ended up selling the same idea to three different parties.

For Chen Guiliang, as long as he got paid, there was no need to cause trouble.

In reality, the most representative figure who made a name for himself with a game idea was that "First Father of China."

A migrant worker with a junior high school education, because he participated in the closed beta for Westward Journey Online II and wrote over 30 pages of feedback and suggestions for improvement, he was appointed as a planner for Westward Journey Online I, and then served as the core planner for Fantasy Westward Journey.

The age of grassroots heroes.

But the premise for all this was that this person had worked as a customer service representative for Westward Journey Online I, and being assigned to the closed beta was part of his job. His opinions could be effectively communicated to the higher-ups at NetEase.

If it were a high school student who rashly went to a big company to peddle a game concept, he would probably be thrown out by security on the spot.

Besides, if Chen Guiliang's game concept were adopted by some big company, it probably wouldn't get him much cash. At most, like the "First Father of China," he would be invited to work in the company's planning department.

What Chen Guiliang was seeking was not a position at a big company.

He wanted to start his own company in the future.

"You study at County No. 2 High School?" Tao Chenggang changed the subject from business to small talk.

Chen Guiliang said, "Third year, humanities experimental class."

Tao Chenggang said, "A top student. My sister also studies at No. 2 High, but she's just in a regular class."

"It's all about the same. To get into No. 2 High, your grades must be excellent," Chen Guiliang said.

They seemed to be chatting idly, but in fact, they had already entered a state of negotiation.

Tao Chenggang, in the tone of an elder, continued to probe, "Which district or county is your hometown in?"

Chen Guiliang said, "Yaojia Township, Fushi County."

"There's an ancient town there, I've visited it," Tao Chenggang asked, "When I was driving past, I saw a Yaojia Bridge on the way. Is that it?"

Chen Guiliang said, "The township market is right at the end of the bridge. My junior high school is on a nearby mountain."

Tao Chenggang smiled, "Next time I go to the ancient town, I'll have you be my guide."

"It would be my honor," Chen Guiliang said.

The two of them sat in the office, chatting on and off.

Yang Yuhui, after a nap, went to the workshop outside to watch the gaming addicts grind, and completed some in-game transactions on the side.

Seeing that Chen Guiliang was just making small talk with him, never bringing up the game, Tao Chenggang understood that Chen Guiliang was no simple character.

Whoever brought up business first would be at a disadvantage.

Because this was a very unconventional deal, both sides were wary of each other, like hitting a wolf with a flimsy pole—scared on both ends.

Tao Chenggang said, "Your ideas are very interesting, but I don't have any plans to make a game."

"Even if the deal falls through, goodwill remains. It was a pleasure to meet you today, Boss Tao," Chen Guiliang said, feigning a retreat. "When winter break comes, I'll take a trip to the coast. Modu, Yangcheng, Pengcheng, Hangcheng... there are game companies in all these big cities. Maybe one of them will be interested."

Tao Chenggang said, "Those big companies are very conservative, and they only know how to license foreign games. The executives don't even play games. Your free-to-play idea is too bold; they won't risk investing in it."

"Who knows? Maybe a blind cat will find a dead mouse," Chen Guiliang said with a smile.

Tao Chenggang put on an air of indifference, stood up, and said, "You sit here for a bit. I'm going to check on the workshop."

Chen Guiliang was left alone in the office.

Tao Chenggang walked outside and immediately took out a cigarette and lit it. He needed to calm down and think.

He ran internet cafes, had dabbled in private servers for Legend of Mir for a while, and was currently running a game workshop. He understood the player psyche very well. If he made a game based on Chen Guiliang's ideas, it could very well become a huge hit.

This was an instinct that the executives at big companies lacked.

The elites at big companies didn't lack money; instead, they valued their time. They would just think it's normal to pay for game time cards. A monthly card only costs a few dozen yuan, while a pay-to-win model would just ruin the game's balance.

But from the perspective of a bottom-tier player?

Wow, this game is free. I can just keep killing monsters and playing without having to buy time cards or a monthly subscription.

Players of later generations found grinding monsters tedious.

But for the vast majority of players at this time, being able to kill monsters without spending money was a form of happiness!

Having run a private server for Legend of Mir, Tao Chenggang could imagine how many free-to-play players a free game could attract. With a massive influx of free-to-play players, the real paying players would also stick around.

What's more, the heap of pay-to-win schemes Chen Guiliang had laid out made Tao Chenggang, a businessman, tingle with excitement.

But here was the problem: Tao Chenggang wasn't a truly big boss, just a small-time tycoon in a remote city.

If he wanted to develop a game himself, he would have to bet his entire fortune, and even then, he'd be short on initial capital.

Should he take the gamble?

What if he failed?

On top of that, he was worried about Chen Guiliang causing trouble.

He was worried that halfway through his game's development, Chen Guiliang would sell the same set of ideas to a big company. He couldn't compete with a big company in terms of operational capability.

Seeing Tao Chenggang standing in the corner in a daze, Yang Yuhui asked, "Gang Ge, what's wrong?"

"It's nothing."

Tao Chenggang said, "You're twenty-eight and still not married. Doesn't your family rush you?"

"You're not married either," Yang Yuhui said irritably. "I'm cooped up in this crappy place all day. Where would I have time to find a girlfriend?"

Tao Chenggang muttered to himself, "Yeah, I'm not married either."

His eight internet cafes, if sold off one by one, could probably fetch around three million yuan.

A house, a new car, mortgaged or sold on the cheap, could bring in another two or three hundred thousand.

He still had nearly four hundred thousand in cash, money he had set aside to open another internet cafe.

It was far from enough.

Perhaps he could manage to create a game, but he wouldn't have money for initial operations and promotion.

He would have to find investors!

Finding a game development team, on the other hand, was easy. Tao Chenggang knew all those tech gurus from the private server scene. He could talk them into joining, and then have them pull in more people.

The game didn't need to be flashy. Even if it was a garbage game, it could become a hit with Chen Guiliang's set of ideas!

Tao Chenggang had a strong gambling streak.

To put it nicely, he was daring and willing to fight for what he wanted.

His parents were just ordinary employees of a state-owned enterprise in Longdu City. Although he never had to worry about food or clothing growing up, they didn't have money to support his entrepreneurial ventures.

This guy graduated from a junior college in 1996, with rather bad luck, just when junior colleges stopped guaranteeing job placements.

His parents pulled some strings to get him into a boiler factory (a state-owned enterprise). It cost them a full 5,000 yuan in bribes, and the manager promised to make him a permanent employee after a year.

But after only three months at the boiler factory, Tao Chenggang quit on his own accord and went to the coastal regions to make his own way.

He went through several jobs before joining Unitech in the summer of 1998, promoting PHS phones in the Yangtze River Delta region. Half a year later, he quit again without warning and switched to distributing IC telephone cards in third and fourth-tier cities.

In just two years, by distributing IC cards, Tao Chenggang earned seven or eight hundred thousand yuan.

As this business gradually saturated the market, Tao Chenggang returned to his hometown to open internet cafes. Then he got into private servers for Legend of Mir, started a game workshop, and even partnered with Feng Tao to sell computers.

He had intended to create a chain of internet cafes, but then Chen Guiliang suddenly threw a set of game ideas at him.

Tao Chenggang was tempted.

He was even getting a little fired up!

This feeling was very similar to when he was selling PHS phones as a salaried worker and accidentally discovered that IC cards were a blue ocean market in third and fourth-tier cities.

It was worth betting his fortune and future on.

Take a gamble, and a bicycle could turn into a motorcycle.

If he really ran out of funds, he could still go back to his old employer, Unitech.

That company had so much money it didn't know where to invest it!

Walking back into the office, Tao Chenggang found Chen Guiliang browsing a forum.

And his actions were outrageously bizarre.

A netizen named absolut (Liu Jiajun, an ancient platinum-level author on Qidian) had posted on the Mengya forum, furiously flaming Guo Xiaosi for being a sissy, which triggered a passionate flame war between the "anti-Guo faction" and the "pro-Guo faction."

And what was Chen Guiliang doing?

Fanning the flames the entire time!

It was because Tao Chenggang hadn't come back for a while, and Chen Guiliang was bored out of his mind, so he had temporarily registered several forum accounts.

With the first account, he posted: "All of you who are cursing Xiaosi are just jealous. Xiaosi is a great contemporary literary master, his talent surpasses Li Bai and Du Fu. Even if you add up all the Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song Dynasties, they wouldn't compare to a single pubic hair on our Xiaosi."

This statement provoked the "anti-Guo faction," instantly drawing a huge wave of angry responses.

Chen Guiliang quickly switched accounts again: "A plagiarist dog has the nerve to call himself a literary master? If I self-published Three Hundred Tang Poems under a different author's name, would that make me the God of Poetry?"

After hitting the enter key, Chen Guiliang switched accounts once more.

Tao Chenggang stood by and watched for a while, a wry expression on his face. What kind of lunatic was this?

Chen Guiliang even turned to ask him, "Boss Tao, want to play for a bit? It's really fun, just like blowing up poop with firecrackers when we were kids."

What a vivid metaphor...

"Ahem!"

Tao Chenggang cleared his throat. "How much are you looking to sell these game ideas for?"

"Three hundred thousand," Chen Guiliang made an exorbitant demand.

Tao Chenggang said, "Do you know what the average salary in Longdu City is?"

Chen Guiliang said, "A few hundred yuan."

Tao Chenggang asked again, "Do you know what the price per unit area of the most expensive housing in Longdu City is?"

"I don't know," Chen Guiliang replied.

"Only 1,300," Tao Chenggang said. "The new residential complexes built in Longdu this year are at most 1,300 yuan per square meter. You're asking for 300,000 right off the bat. That can buy two high-end commercial apartments of over a hundred square meters. My internet cafe only cost three or four hundred thousand to set up!"

Chen Guiliang said, "Then 250,000. I promise that after I sell these papers to you, I will not approach any big company."

"At most, it's worth ten thousand yuan," Tao Chenggang lowballed him.

Chen Guiliang said while typing a post, "200,000. I'll give you some more detailed suggestions. Those papers aren't clear enough. For example, about game shills and such."

"Game shills?" Tao Chenggang's first reaction was that they were similar to medical shills or alcohol shills.

Amidst the clatter of typing, Chen Guiliang switched accounts and posted another inflammatory thread.

He let go of the keyboard and said, "Don't disband this workshop of yours. Have them go into the game and be shills. Some of them can pretend to be girls and start online relationships with the whale players. Have others act as underlings for the whales, instigating hatred and fights among them. With women, brothers, and enemies, fill their lives with love, hate, passion, and vengeance, then you won't have to worry about the whales not spending money to boost their combat power, will you?"

Dude, he's not hitting my ass, he's slapping your face!

Tao Chenggang looked at the flame-baiting, poop-stirring post on the forum, then carefully considered what Chen Guiliang had said about game shills.

Different methods, same result.

Damn, that makes a lot of sense!

How does this high school student's brain work?

But it still wasn't enough to make Tao Chenggang willingly cough up the money. He looked at Chen Guiliang, who was still posting, "What other good ideas do you have?"

"Lotteries."

Chen Guiliang hit the enter key and said, "Before private lotteries were restricted, there were stalls everywhere for scratch-off tickets. Even farmers who came to the city to sell vegetables couldn't resist buying a couple."

"You can set up a lottery system in the game. Regardless of whether a player has paid or not, they get one free draw every day. Use the daily free draw to attract players. The second draw and onwards will cost money. Set up some top-tier equipment, display it on the lottery interface. The more consecutive draws, the higher the probability of getting something good. You can also have things like ten-draws, twenty-draws, and set a guaranteed good item for a certain number of draws..."

Tao Chenggang recalled the crazy lottery scenes by the roadside in the 90s and thought to himself: This lottery system alone could get gamers hooked.

"What else?" Tao Chenggang continued to inquire.

But Chen Guiliang stopped talking. "It's like the game lottery. Those two ideas just now were a free bonus. The rest will cost you. As long as you pay up, Boss Tao, I will tell you everything I know, holding nothing back."

Tao Chenggang fell silent, thinking.
